articles.title: ‘Tetsuo’ Director Tsukamoto Shinya on Staying Independent and Why He Can’t Pull Away From War Films
articles.summary: Beloved independent filmmaker Tsukamoto Shinya gave a masterclass at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF), speaking about the pivotal works of his career as well as his most recent film, the English-language feature “Mr.
body: Tsukamoto recalled shooting the film on 16mm, before the era of digital VFX.

“No CG. We had a little bit of tokusatsu [practical special effects] technology at the time but this didn’t use any of that, this used stuff which was thrown out on the street and we basically stuck it on [Taguchi Tomorowo]’s face,” the director said. Of the effect of Taguchi gliding through the streets, he said to “think of it as really rough stop motion.”

The film took about a year to make, Tsukamoto said, though “the time we spent with the crew was shorter, a lot of the time towards the end I was working alone – like the sparks flying off at the end [of the clip], that was something I worked on alone.”
The success of “Tetsuo,” he said, took him to film festivals overseas and led to his second feature, the horror film “Hiruko the Goblin,” now with a higher budget.

articles.title: Elena Maganini, Film Editor on ‘Dexter,’ ‘Henry, Portrait of a Serial Killer,’ Dies at 70
articles.summary: Elena Maganini, a TV and film editor who won an Emmy for cutting the pilot for “Dexter” and edited several films for director John McNaughton, died Oct. 21 in Burbank of complications from breast cancer. She was 70. Born in Chicago, she graduated from the U.
body: Her first feature credit came for McNaughton’s influential 1986 “Henry, Portrait of a Serial Killer.” She went on to edit McNaughton films including “Wild Things,” which starred Matt Dillon, Neve Campbell and Kevin Bacon, “Mad Dog & Glory” and “Sex, Drugs and Rock & Roll,” “The Borrower,” “Speaking of Sex” and “Lansky.” Other feature credits include “Next Friday” and “Ed Gein.”

Moving into television, Maganini edited the pilot for “Dexter,” for which she won an Emmy, and went on to edit shows including “Madam Secretary,” “Good Behavior,” “Clarice,” “Manifest” and “The Cleaning Lady.” She was nominated for an Emmy and a Cable ACE Award for “If These Walls Could Talk,” an anthology about abortion directed by Cher and Nancy Savoca and starring Catherine Keener, Demi Moore and Shirley Knight.
Survivors include husband Scott Collins, communications director at Motion Picture Editors Guild; daughter Gabriella Coronel; and daughter-in-law Adrienne Coronel.
A memorial service will be held Nov. 15 at 1 p.m. at the Fine Arts Theatre in Beverly Hills. Donations may be made to Columbia College Chicago, Tree House Humane Society or the Stray Cat Alliance.

articles.title: Cynthia Nixon Says She ‘Loved’ Miranda’s Attempts to Become ‘Woke’ on ‘And Just Like That’ Despite Fans Being ‘Horrified’
articles.summary: Cynthia Nixon is standing by her “Sex and the City” character Miranda Hobbes’ arc in the chaotic reboot “And Just Like That” — despite how bewildering some fans found it.
body: While Hobbes underwent several personal shifts in the reboot of the iconic 6 Season HBO drama, the most contentious point for audiences was her relationship with comedian Che Diaz, whom she left her husband, Steve Brady, for in Season 1. In the original series, Hobbes, a lawyer, met Brady, a bartender, in Season 2, then broke up, ultimately got back together, got married, and welcomed a child, Brady Hobbes, by the show’s end.

Nixon also spoke of how she was swayed to reprise the role of Hobbes in the reboot to begin with. “I became convinced that we could really do interesting, dangerous things,” she said. “And that we could make up for some of our past mistakes, the chief one being that it was such an overwhelmingly white show.” And while reactions to the show were always a mixed bag, Nixon admits she was caught off guard when she learned “And Just Like That” wouldn’t be returning for a fourth season: “I was not at all ready,” she said. “Not at all.”

Currently, Nixon stars in HBO’s historical drama “The Gilded Age” as Ada Forte. The show debuted in Jan. 2022 and has run for three subsequent seasons. Season 4 premiered on Sunday on HBO and HBO Max.

articles.title: 'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?
articles.summary: The slang term, which relates to outshining or upstaging someone, is one of 10 words celebrated.
body: "Mogging", a word used playfully to mean outshining, outperforming or upstaging someone or something, has been named as word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary.
A fast-growing slang word among members of Generations Z and Alpha - both online and in everyday conversation - mogging went mainstream in 2026 with a 210% increase in its usage.
Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft said its lexicographers look at "how often words are used" and also "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.
The selection of mogging as word of the year, he said, "shows how each generation leaves its mark on language".

articles.title: ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Director Matsubayashi Yoju on a 10-Year Journey Tracing Brazilian Dancers’ Island Roots
articles.summary: Exploring the relationship between people and place, new documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” playing at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival as part of its Nippon Cinema Now selection, was born from director Matsubayashi Yoju’s time with a Brazilian community of Okinawan immigrants some 10 years…
body: “In 2016 I had the opportunity to live in Brazil for one year. At the time I was trying to work on this other project about Fukushima, but it wasn’t going well so I just decided to, you know, lay back and just have beers in the morning, etc.,” Matsubayashi says. “That’s when I actually found out about the forced relocation of Japanese Brazilians in Santos in Brazil.”
That wartime relocation, in which some 60% of the Japanese immigrants forced out were from Okinawa, became the focus of Matsubayashi’s 2020 documentary “Okinawa/Santos.”

“After that, I was exposed to the Urizunkai,” he says. “This is the Brazilian Okinawa community there, and so I happened to get to know them, and then I found out that they are sending Okinawa Brazilians to Okinawa for training and scholarship. So that’s actually the starting point of the project.”

articles.title: David Bowie's Scottish links celebrated in new exhibition
articles.summary: Hundreds of items from Bowie's personal archive are set to go on display at the V&A in Dundee.
body: As musician Nile Rodgers once noted, David Bowie did not just make art - he was art.
So it is apt that his life and work should be celebrated in the V&A Dundee, within earshot of the first venue he played in Scotland under his new stage name.
David Bowie and the Buzz were not even the headline act that night at the Palais de Dans in 1966, but it was the start of a relationship with Scottish fans which continues today.
David Bowie: On Tour is the first exhibition to showcase items from the singer's archive, which was acquired by the V&A in London in 2023.

articles.title: One in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting again
articles.summary: Following a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformed. There’s a startling moment in this BBC refugee documentary when Syrian mother Nisreen – in the apparently miserable situation of hiking across the Balkans towards Germany, four kids in…
body: Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ superb, forthright and highly moving film bypasses the usual refugee dichotomies, that they’re either external threats or history’s victims. Instead of flat abstractions, we get the knotty reality. Focused over a 10-year period from 2015 to 2025 principally on Nisreen’s eldest daughter Israa, it presents an intimate chronicle of how geographical displacement and cultural dislocation reshape families and lives from the inside.

It’s a wrenchingly immediate demonstration of the neglected flip side to discussions of how immigrants alter host countries – and how the immigrants themselves are also changed in the process. Through the young man who becomes her husband, Israa slowly comes to a rapprochement with her Syrian and Muslim identity – and finally makes an Ithacan return to Aleppo. But the damage is harder to repair for once-respected shawarma chef Tarek, who in his own moment of truth admits he made his family pay for his loss of status. As his daughter says at the start: “War is not as hard as what comes after.”

articles.title: ‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disaster
articles.summary: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher.
body: Taika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from a Kazuo Ishiguro novel.
In a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”
He added: “The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit … Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Pointing to the disparity of the film’s audience and critics’ score on review aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes, which currently stands at 74% for the former and 26% (from 90 reviews) for the latter, Waititi also wrote: “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people.”

articles.title: A Royal Surprise: ‘The Remarried Empress’ Releases One Day Early on Disney+ and Hulu
articles.summary: The wildly anticipated Korean fantasy romance, starring Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk and Lee Se-young, will launch with four episodes Nov. 3, followed by two new installments every Wednesday.
body: In a surprise gift to fans, Disney + and Hulu are moving up the royal arrival of The Remarried Empress, bringing the lavish Korean fantasy romance to viewers Nov. 3, one day ahead of its previously announced premiere.

Stars Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk and Lee Se-young revealed the change Tuesday at a press conference in Seoul. The first four episodes will be available at launch, with Disney describing the early release as a thank you to fans for their support.

Based on the hit Naver Webtoon, The Remarried Empress combines palace intrigue, romantic betrayal and an impossibly elegant heroine determined to claim her own future. Shin plays Navier, the empress of the Eastern Empire, whose marriage unravels when her husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju), falls for escaped slave girl Rashta (Lee Se-young). Navier agrees to his request for a divorce on one condition: She must be permitted to marry her own budding love — Crown Prince Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk) of the rival Western Kingdom.
The series was adapted for the screen by Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol and directed by Cho Suwon, whose credits include Still 17 and Pinocchio.

articles.title: Blockhead review – struggling novelist embraces his inner monster in comic thriller of literary machismo
articles.summary: Writer-director Matt Harlock looks into ego and insecurity in a smart film about a BritLit bad boy who goes down a grisly road. This has nothing to do with Ian Dury; rather, it is a brisk, effective British indie thriller informed by the legend of Robert Louis Stevenson wrestling his shadow self…
body: No prizes, then, for guessing which David Fincher film provides the template here. Typing to a soundtrack of his own best reviews (“The world needs to hear your story”), an emboldened Will is soon exploring grislier avenues, including home invasion and murder, while his increasingly unhinged rants to creative-writing students attract a rapt protege. Evoking a world where publishers push books with unequivocally positive pull quotes like “confrontational” and “dangerous”, Harlock is taking a red pencil to hackneyed notions of bad-boy writers. There is, he posits, only so much muscle one can wield while hunched over a laptop.
